title: How to count your menstrual cycle
summary: What to record, how cycle length is counted and why a calendar cannot confirm ovulation.

sections.heading: Start with the first day of bleeding
paragraphs: The first day of your period is day one of a new cycle. Cycle length is the number of days from that date to the first day of your next period.
Recording several cycles shows your usual pattern more clearly than a single date.

sections.heading: Expect some variation
paragraphs: Periods can change with contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding, stress and the approach to menopause. An estimate based on your previous cycle may not match your next one.
Ovulation timing also varies, so a period calendar cannot confirm ovulation or reliably prevent pregnancy.

sections.heading: Record symptoms as well as dates
paragraphs: Note bleeding duration, pain, bleeding between periods and any effect on sleep, work or usual activities. Bring these notes to a healthcare appointment if symptoms change or concern you.
If pregnancy is possible and your period is late, follow the instructions on a pregnancy test and contact a clinician if you need advice.

title: Period changes to discuss with a clinician
summary: Heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods and pain that affects daily life deserve assessment.

sections.heading: Notice the effect on daily life
paragraphs: Needing to change period products very frequently, passing large clots or bleeding through clothes can be signs of heavy periods. Feeling persistently tired or short of breath is also worth discussing because heavy bleeding can lead to iron deficiency.
You do not need to wait until symptoms become severe before booking an appointment.

sections.heading: Describe what has changed
paragraphs: Tell a clinician about bleeding between periods, bleeding after sex, a new change in cycle pattern or pain that stops you doing normal activities. Any bleeding after menopause needs medical assessment.
Record when symptoms started, any contraception or medicines you use and whether pregnancy is possible.

sections.heading: Get urgent help for severe symptoms
paragraphs: Seek urgent medical help for severe bleeding with faintness, collapse or difficulty breathing. Sudden severe abdominal pain, particularly with bleeding or a possible pregnancy, also needs urgent assessment.
Call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department if symptoms are severe or you feel unsafe waiting.

title: Prepare for your first antenatal appointment
summary: How to arrange care, what the first appointment may cover and what to bring.

sections.heading: Arrange care after a positive test
paragraphs: Contact your local maternity service or primary care clinician after a positive pregnancy test. Getting in touch early gives you time to discuss screening and other care that may need to happen at particular stages of pregnancy.
How you register for care depends on where you live.

sections.heading: Expect questions about your health
paragraphs: The first appointment usually covers your health history, previous pregnancies, medicines, mental health and any support you need. Your care team will explain the checks and screening available locally.
Ask what each test is for, when results will arrive and who to contact with questions.

sections.heading: Bring dates, medicines and questions
paragraphs: Write down the first day of your last period if you know it, your medicines and supplements, allergies and the questions you want answered. Discuss prescribed medicines with a clinician rather than stopping them on your own.
Do not wait for a booked appointment if you develop severe abdominal pain, fainting or concerning bleeding; seek urgent medical advice.

title: Managing questions in early pregnancy
summary: Common symptoms, medicine checks and when nausea or pain needs medical attention.

sections.heading: Symptoms differ between pregnancies
paragraphs: Tiredness, nausea, breast tenderness and needing to urinate more often can occur in early pregnancy. The presence or absence of these symptoms cannot confirm how a pregnancy is progressing.
Ask your maternity team about symptoms you are unsure of rather than using a symptom list to judge the pregnancy.

sections.heading: Ask for help if you cannot keep fluids down
paragraphs: Nausea and vomiting can become serious when they prevent you from eating or drinking. Contact a clinician if you cannot keep fluids down, pass much less urine, feel very dizzy or are losing weight.
Treatments are available, and a clinician can assess dehydration and other possible causes.

sections.heading: Check medicines and know urgent symptoms
paragraphs: Ask a clinician or pharmacist about any prescription medicines, over-the-counter treatments or supplements you take. Your maternity team can explain nutrition, activity and local screening recommendations.
Severe or one-sided abdominal pain, fainting or heavy bleeding needs urgent medical assessment, even if you have not yet had your first appointment.

title: Physical recovery after giving birth
summary: What to monitor during recovery and which symptoms need urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Follow changes in bleeding, pain and wounds
paragraphs: Bleeding and discharge usually reduce gradually after birth, and recovery differs after vaginal and caesarean birth. Tell your maternity team about increasing pain, foul-smelling discharge or a wound that becomes red, swollen or starts leaking.
Keep the follow-up appointments recommended by your care team, even if you feel well.

sections.heading: Plan practical help
paragraphs: Help with meals, laundry and other children can make it easier to rest and attend appointments. Keep food and water accessible and ask for feeding support if feeds are painful or difficult.
Discuss returning to exercise, sex or other activities with your clinician if you have pain, complications or questions about healing.

sections.heading: Do not delay urgent assessment
paragraphs: Severe bleeding, chest pain, breathing difficulty, seizures or a severe headache with visual changes after birth require urgent medical help. Fever with feeling unwell also needs prompt assessment because infection can worsen quickly.
For severe symptoms, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department and tell staff that you recently gave birth.

title: Getting help with mood changes after birth
summary: How to ask for support with anxiety, depression or symptoms that feel unsafe.

sections.heading: Take changes in mood seriously
paragraphs: Feeling tearful or overwhelmed can happen after birth, but strong, persistent feelings or difficulty managing daily tasks deserve support. Depression and anxiety can begin during pregnancy or after birth, with or without an obvious cause.
You do not have to wait for a particular number of days before asking for help.

sections.heading: Tell someone what is happening
paragraphs: Contact a midwife, primary care clinician or mental health professional and describe your sleep, mood, worries and ability to care for yourself. A trusted person can help you make contact and attend an appointment.
Support may include practical help, talking therapies and medicines discussed with a clinician, including any questions about feeding your baby.

sections.heading: Treat unsafe or unusual symptoms as urgent
paragraphs: Seek immediate help for thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, hearing or seeing things others do not, severe confusion or rapidly worsening symptoms. These can require urgent specialist treatment.
Call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department, and ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby while help is arranged.

title: Check how newborn feeding is going
summary: Feeding cues, questions to bring to a feeding review and signs a baby needs assessment.

sections.heading: Watch cues and behaviour
paragraphs: Early hunger cues can include turning the head to look for a feed, opening the mouth and bringing hands to the mouth. Crying can be a later sign, so it helps to notice the earlier cues.
Ask your midwife or baby care team what to expect for your baby, especially if they were born early or have a health condition.

sections.heading: Ask about pain, nappies and weight
paragraphs: Seek feeding support if breastfeeding hurts, attachment is difficult or bottle feeds are consistently hard to manage. Your care team can assess feeding, weight change and whether the number of wet nappies is appropriate for your baby’s age.
If using formula, follow the product instructions and local health guidance for preparation rather than changing the powder-to-water ratio.

sections.heading: Get help for poor feeding or unusual sleepiness
paragraphs: Contact a clinician promptly if a baby feeds much less than usual, has fewer wet nappies than expected, repeatedly vomits or is unusually sleepy. A baby who is difficult to wake or has breathing difficulty needs urgent assessment.
For severe symptoms or blue or grey skin, call your local emergency number immediately.

title: Set up a safer sleep space
summary: Back sleeping, a clear cot and a firm, flat surface are the main starting points.

sections.heading: Use the back position for every sleep
paragraphs: Place your baby on their back for every sleep on a firm, flat mattress in a cot, crib or bassinet designed for infant sleep. Inclined sleepers and sleep-positioning products are not substitutes for a safe sleep surface.
If your baby has a medical condition, ask their clinician about any individual instructions.

sections.heading: Keep the sleep surface clear
paragraphs: Keep pillows, duvets, cot bumpers, loose bedding and soft toys out of the sleep space. Follow local safer-sleep guidance on suitable bedding, clothing and room temperature.
Do not cover your baby’s head during sleep or allow them to become overheated.

sections.heading: Plan where you will put a sleepy baby
paragraphs: NHS guidance recommends a separate sleep space in your room for the first six months. Sofas and armchairs are particularly dangerous places to fall asleep with a baby.
If you feel sleepy while feeding or holding your baby, put them back in their own sleep space before you fall asleep.

sources.label: NHS: Helping your baby to sleep

title: Use a baby milestone checklist
summary: Record examples of new skills and bring concerns to your child’s healthcare team.

sections.heading: Look across different types of skills
paragraphs: Development includes movement, communication, learning and social interaction. A checklist can help you record what your child does during everyday play and care.
Write down examples and dates rather than relying only on a total number of checked boxes.

sections.heading: Use the checklist to start a conversation
paragraphs: Milestone lists are not diagnostic tests, and the age calculator on this site cannot assess development. If your child was born early, ask their clinician how corrected age should be used when discussing skills.
Bring your notes, questions and any relevant videos to routine developmental appointments.

sections.heading: Raise concerns when you notice them
paragraphs: Contact your child’s healthcare team if you are concerned about development rather than waiting for every item on a checklist. Tell them promptly if your child loses a skill they previously used.
The team can discuss developmental screening, hearing or vision checks and any further assessment that may be useful.

title: Prepare for a healthcare appointment
summary: A short symptom record, medicine list and clear questions can make an appointment more useful.

sections.heading: Describe the pattern
paragraphs: Write down when each symptom started, how often it happens, what makes it better or worse and how it affects daily life. If bleeding is part of the concern, include dates, duration and any change from your usual pattern.
Start the appointment with the problem you most want help with.

sections.heading: Bring the details you may forget
paragraphs: Bring a list of medicines and supplements, allergies, relevant test results and your main questions. Ask in advance if you need an interpreter, communication support or another adjustment.
You can ask what an examination involves and discuss consent, comfort and alternatives before it begins.

sections.heading: Leave with a clear next step
paragraphs: Ask what the plan is, when to expect results and who to contact if you have not heard back. Check which symptoms should lead you to seek help sooner.
If an explanation is unclear, ask the clinician to use different words or write down the key points.
